subject: how to vectorize model with year-specific effects

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: how to vectorize model with year-specific effects
parts:
Hi,

I am running the following model:

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
data {
int<lower=1> N_observation; // number of observations
int<lower=1> N_year; // number of years
real dlogw[N_observation]; // change in log wage
int<lower=1, upper=N_year> year_index[N_observation];
// the year for each observation
}
parameters {
real year_mean[N_year]; // mean for each year
real<lower=0> year_var[N_year]; // variance for each year
}
model {
for (i in 1:N_observation) {
dlogw ~ normal(year_mean[year_index[i]], sqrt(year_var[year_index[i]]));
}
}
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

with N_year=29 and N_observation=36270. It is somewhat slow. Is there
any way I can make it faster, eg by vectorization? Could not figure out
how to do that in this context.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: how to vectorize model with year-specific effects
parts:
I think I found a solution:

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
model {
real mean_[N_observation];
real sd_[N_observation];

mean_[i] <- year_mean[year_index[i]];
sd_[i] <- sqrt(year_var[year_index[i]]);
}
dlogw ~ normal(mean_, sd_);
}
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

is about 700x faster (!).

Can someone please explain why? Is it really the vectorization of the
normal? I thought the normal was a cheap operation. It seems I do not
yet have a good mental model of Stan.

Is factoring out deterministic parts into a loop so that I can vectorize
distributions a good strategy in Stan in general?

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: how to vectorize model with year-specific effects
parts:
Every time you add a distribution to your model you introduce a bit of overhead, both in actually computing the density and its gradient with our autodiff code.  For large models (tens of thousands of observations counts as reasonably big) this overhead is significant.

When you vectorize, however, that overhead is drastically slashed.  For example, we can share intermediate evaluations and avoid redundant calculation.  The biggest gain is from the autodiff overhead -- and given the number of observations you have a few orders of magnitude improvement is not surprising.

So, yes, having lots of deterministic temporaries in memory to admit vectorization is worth it given the way Stan works under the hood.
